Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilq.qov.ph DILG OPINION No. 130 s. 2021 DEC 2021 HON. ROMULO L. ACDAL Elected Vice-Mayor Paoay, Ilocos Norte Dear Hon. Acdal: This has reference to your letter dated November 29, 2021, with attachments, requesting the DILG Secretary's immediate action to install you as the official Mayor of Paoay, Ilocos Note in order to discharge fully all the duties and responsibilities appertaining to said office. Based on the documents forwarded to the Central Office, it appears that in 2016 elections, Jessie Galano (Mayor Galano) was elected as Mayor of Paoay, Ilocos Norte. In the 2019 local elections, he was re-elected as Mayor while you were elected as Vice-Mayor. By Decision dated January 31, 2018, Mayor Galano was dismissed from the service with its accessory penalties by the Office of the Ombudsman (OMB). He availed various legal remedies before the Court of Appeals (CA) and the Supreme Court (SC). The CA affirmed the Decision of the OMB. Mayor Galano sought refuge from the SC. By Resolution dated June 19, 2019 in G.R. No. 246397 entitled "Galano vs. Martires, et al.," the SC denied Mayor Galano's petition for failure to show that the CA committed reversible error in rendering its assailed dispositions as to warrant the exercise of the SC's discretionary appellate jurisdiction. Mayor Galano filed a Motion for Reconsideration thereto and in a Resolution dated July 07, 2021, the SC denied the same with finality, thus: "WHEREFORE, the motion for reconsideration is DENIED with FINALITY. No further pleadings or motions shall be entertained in this case. Let entry of judgment be issued immediately. SO ORDERED." You, who consider yourself as "OIC" of the Office of the Mayor since July 4, 2019, comes before the Department asking the DILG Secretary to install you as the official Mayor of Paoay, Ilocos Norte. Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

At the outset, this level deems it necessary to clarify the nomenclature you have given to yourself, that is, as "OIC" since July 4, 2019. The term "OIC" or "officer-in-charge" in the Office of the Mayor can be found in Section 46 (c) of Republic Act No. 7160 or the Local Govemment Code of 1991, thus: "SECTION 46. Temporary Vacancy in the Office of the Local Chief Executive. x x x x (c) When the incumbent local chief executive is traveling within the country but outside his territorial jurisdiction for a period not exceeding three (3) consecutive days, he may designate in writing the officer-in-charge of the said office. Such authorization shall specify the powers and functions that the local official concemed shall exercise in the absence of the local chief executive except the power to appoint, suspend, or dismiss employees. xxx xxx Section 46 (c) above presupposes a situation where the local chief executive, like the Municipal Mayor, is traveling within the country but outside his territorial jurisdiction for a period not exceeding three (3) consecutive days, in which case, an OIC of the office of the local chief executive may be designated. It is clear from the foregoing that an OIC of the office of the local chief executive can only be designated if the incumbent local chief executive is traveling within the country but outside his/her territorial jurisdiction for a period not longer than three (3) consecutive days. In the herein case, the reason for Mayor Galano's absence was due to his dismissal from the service, he was not travelling. Accordingly, Section 46 (c) and the use of the nomenclature "OIC" is not proper in the case at hand when you are referring to the one acting as Mayor in the absence of the elected Mayor. Going back to your primary concern, previously, this Department held the view, out of prudence, that dismissal from the service wherein the respondent local elective official availed or has pending legal remedies before the Office of the Ombudsman, the Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court assailing his dismissal order, is a temporary vacancy, not permanent, since the elected vice-mayor or next —in-rank's assumption to the Office of the Mayor or concerned office is still subject to the outcome of the aforesaid remedies availed of by the respondent elective official. However, the aforesaid view of the Department was corrected by the SC in Tallado vs. COMELEC, et al.' in this manner: "xxx inasmuch as Section 46 of the LGC textually applied to succession where the local chief executive was 'temporarily incapacitated to perform his duties for physical or legal reasons such as, but not limited to, leave of absence, travel abroad, and suspension from office,' the provision was certainly not the proper basis for the COMELEC to characterize as temporary the vacancy in the 1 G.R. No. 246679, September 10, 2019. Page 2 of

office of Governor ensuing from the petitioner's dismissal. As earlier explained. the vacancy was not temporary because the petitioner was fully divested of his title to the office of the Governor in both instances of his dismissal. Under Section 44 of the LGC, a permanent vacancy arises whenever an elective local official fills a higher vacant office, or refuses to assume office, or fails to qualify, or dies, or is removed from office, or voluntarily resigns, or is otherwise permanently incapacitated to discharge the functions of his office. In contrast, Section 46 of the LGC enumerates as resulting in a temporary vacancy in the office of the local chief executive leave of absence, travel abroad, and suspension from office. Although Section 46 of the LGC specifically states that the causes of a temporary vacancy are not limited to such circumstances, what is evident is that the enumeration therein share something in common, which is that there is a definite term to be re-assumed. However, the petitioner's dismissals, even if still not final were akin to the instances enumerated in Section 56 of the LGC because the loss of his title to the office denied to him the expectancy to re-assume his term. Lastly, Section 44 of the LGC includes removal from office as one of the instances triggering a permanent vacancy. Such permanent vacancy was precisely the outcome that the OMB directed in its decisions. Consequently, when the petitioner was ousted in the period from November 8, 2016 to December 30, 2016, in the first instance of dismissal, and in the period from March 14, 2018 to September 26, 2018, in the second instance of dismissal, the permanent vacancy in the office of the Governor ensued." (Emphasis Supplied) This was reiterated in the SC Resolution dated March 2, 2021 in the same case, which resolved the motions for reconsideration filed by the private respondents and the Commission on Elections (COMELEC), thus: "In Our September IO, 2019 Decision, this Court ruled that the dismissal orders of the OMB against petitioner serves as permanent removal from office and was not merely temporary. From his dismissal until the Court of Appeals' modification of his penalty to suspension, petitioner neither had title nor powers to wield as governor of Camarines Norte. As evidence of this lack of title by petitioner, Camarines Vice Governor Jonah Pedro G. Pimentel was sworn as Governor, and not as Acting Governor. The nomenclature used here by the Department of the Interior and Local Govemment (DILG) is important because it recognizes that the vacancy is not temporary but a permanent one. To rule otherwise would result in the absurd situation where a public office is occupied by two persons when basic in the law on public officers is that in single constituency positions, like the Office of the Provincial Governor, only one person can occupy a public office at a given time. The fact that the DILG has now clarified its position that it should have applied Section 46 of the Local Govemment Code, rather than Sec. 44, is irrelevant. As stated earlier, it is not the position of the DILG to characterize the nature of the dismissal of public officers being merely the implementor of the law." Having clarified that the dismissal ordered by the Office of the Ombudsman albeit with pending legal remedies would result to permanent vacancy, not temporary, we Page 3 of

deem it proper to cite Section 44 (a) of the Local Govemment Code of 1991 , viz: "SECTION 44. Permanent Vacancies in the Offices of the Govemor, Vice- Governor, Mayor, and Vice-Mayor. — (a) If a permanent vacancy occurs in the office of the governor or mayor, the vice-govemor or vice-mayor concerned shall become the govemor or mayor. If a permanent vacancy occurs in the offices of the governor, vice-governor, mayor, or vice-mayor, the highest ranking sanggunian member or, in case of his permanent inability, the second highest ranking sanggunian member, shall become the governor, vice-governor, mayor or vice-mayor, as the case may be. Subsequent vacancies in the said office shall be filled automatically by the other sanqqunian members accordinq to their ranking as defined herein." (Emphasis Supplied) Based on the aforequoted provision of law, the vice-mayor shall become the mayor if permanent vacancy occurs in the latter's office. Said assumption of the vice-mayor is automatic or by operation of law and therefore needs no further overt act. Such being the case, we find your request for the DILG Secretary to officially install you as Mayor of Paoay, Ilocos Norte after the dismissal of elected Mayor Galano no longer necessary as it is not even required under the law. Along this line, after your assumption to the Office of the Mayor o, the first-ranking Sangguniang Bayan (SB) member shall assume as Vice-Mayor while subsequent vacancies shall be filled automatically by the other sanggunian members according to their ranking. The resultant vacancy in the 8th position shall be appointed in accordance with Section 45 of the Local Government Code of 1991 , which reads: "Section 45. Permanent Vacancies in the Sanggunian. — (a) Permanent vacancies in the sanggunian where automatic succession provided above do not apply shall be filled by appointment in the following manner: (1) The President, through the Executive Secretary, in the case of the sangguniang panlalawigan and the sangguniang panlungsod of highly urbanized cities and independent component cities; (2) The governor. in the case of the sangguniang panlungsod of component cities and the sanqqunianq bayan; (3) The city or municipal mayor, in the case of sangguniang barangay, upon recommendation of the sangguniang barangay concerned. (b) Except for the sangguniang barangay, only the nominee of the political party under which the sanggunian member concerned had been elected and whose elevation to the position next higher in rank created the last vacancy in the sanggunian shall be appointed in the manner hereinabove provided. The appointee shall come from the same political party as that of the sanggunian member who caused the vacancy and shall serve the unexpired term of the vacant office. In the appointment herein mentioned, a nomination and a certificate of membership of the appointee from the highest official of the political party concemed are conditions sine qua non, and any appointment without such Page 4 of

nomination and certification shall be null and void ab initio and shall be a ground for administrative action against the official responsible therefore. (c) In case or permanent vacancy is caused by a sanggunian member who does not belong to any political party, the local chief executive shall, upon recommendation of the sanggunian concerned, appoint a qualified person to fill the vacancy. (d) In case of vacancy in the representation of the youth and the barangay in the sanggunian, said vacancy shall be filled automatically by the official next in rank of the organization concemed." (Emphasis Supplied) In the landmark case of Navarro vs. CA2, the SC rules that the "last vacancy/' mentioned in Section 45 (b) of the Local Government Code of 1991 is neither the vacancy caused by the elevation of the Vice-Mayor to the Office of the Mayor nor the vacancy left by the last ranking sanggunian member when he was elevated to the 7th ranking position, but rather it is that vacancy caused by the elevation of the 1st-ranking sanggunian member to the next higher rank, i.e., the Vice-Mayor, by reason of succession. The Supreme Court ratiocinated that the reason behind the right given to a political party to nominate a replacement where a permanent vacancy occurs in the sanggunian is to maintain the party representation as willed by the people in the election. This Department believes that in electoral democracy, conscientious people may choose candidates not only because of their personal attributes and qualifications but also because of their political party affiliation. Accordingly, in the Navarro case, the political party nomination should be issued by the political party of the senior sanggunian member because he was the one who caused the last vacancy in the sanggunian due to his elevation as vice-mayor. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have assisted you accordingly. Thank you.
